items.title: Mia's Diary 4: My first window display
items.dek: Monday: Mia has a new job at the bookshop, and she has never done it before.
paragraphs: Monday, 23 November 2026. It is cold today, and I have just come home from work. I have made a big cup of tea, so now I can write.
This morning Helen asked me, “Mia, have you ever made a window display?” “No, never,” I said. “Good,” she said. “Today is your first time!” The theme is “Winter Stories”.
I have already chosen ten books. There is a book about snow, a story about a polar bear, and Sam's favourite book about the sea. Sam has just helped me carry the boxes to the window.
I felt a little nervous. I have never done anything like this before! Helen said, “Don't worry. Have you ever seen a bad window on Park Street? No? Then yours will be fine.”
At four o'clock, a woman stopped and looked at the window. Then she came in and bought the polar bear book. Helen smiled. “You have already sold a book, and you haven't even finished!”

On my way home I met Mr Patel. Biscuit has just jumped in a puddle, and he was very muddy. “Have you ever seen such a dirty dog?” asked Mr Patel. “No, never!” I said. Tomorrow I will buy some small lights for the window.
paragraphs_zh: 2026年11月23日，星期一。今天很冷，我刚刚下班回到家。我已经泡了一大杯茶，所以现在可以写日记了。
今天早上，海伦问我：“米娅，你做过橱窗展示吗？”“没有，从来没做过。”我说。“很好，”她说，“今天是你的第一次！”主题是“冬日故事”。
我已经选好了十本书。有一本关于雪的书，一个关于北极熊的故事，还有萨姆最爱的那本关于大海的书。萨姆刚刚帮我把箱子搬到橱窗那边。
我有一点紧张。我以前从来没做过这样的事！海伦说：“别担心。你在公园街上见过难看的橱窗吗？没有吧？那你的也不会差。”
四点钟，一位女士停下来看橱窗。然后她走进店里，买了那本北极熊的书。海伦笑了。“你已经卖出一本书了，而且你还没做完呢！”
回家的路上，我遇到了帕特尔先生。饼干刚刚跳进了一个水坑，浑身是泥。“你见过这么脏的狗吗？”帕特尔先生问。“没有，从来没见过！”我说。明天我要买一些小灯挂在橱窗里。

glossary.en: the things a shop puts in its front window for people to see
a little afraid or worried before something important
to take something from one place to another in your hands
a big white bear that lives in the cold north
a small pool of water on the ground after rain
used to say something is surprising or very small

items.grammar: Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) to talk about your life up to now, or about something that happened a short time ago. Ever and never show experience: “Have you ever made a window display?” “No, never.” Just means a very short time ago, and already means earlier than you thought: “Sam has just helped me”, “I have already chosen ten books”.
items.grammar_zh: 现在完成时（have/has + 过去分词）用来说“到现在为止”的经历，或刚刚发生的事。ever 和 never 表示经历：“Have you ever made a window display?”（你做过橱窗展示吗？）“No, never.”（没有，从来没有。）just 表示“刚刚”，already 表示“已经”：“Sam has just helped me”（萨姆刚刚帮了我），“I have already chosen ten books”（我已经选好了十本书）。和汉语的“过”“已经”“刚”有点像，但英语不用具体的过去时间词，比如不能说 yesterday。
questions: What has Mia never done before?
Why does Helen smile at four o'clock?
And you? Have you ever done something new at work or school? What was it?

items.title: The cardiologist and the gig
items.dek: In Rest of World, the scholar Julián Posada argues that AI is not so much abolishing skilled work as breaking it into piecework, and that the template was drawn years ago in Venezuela.
paragraphs: The usual fear about artificial intelligence is that it will make professionals redundant. Julián Posada, an assistant professor at Yale and the author of a book on what he calls platform extractivism, proposes a less cinematic but arguably grimmer outcome in an essay for Rest of World published on 19 November. Expertise, he suggests, is not disappearing; it is being repackaged as gig work, priced task by task and terminable at a click.

The figures he gathers make the hierarchy plain. Outlier, a recruiting platform run by Scale AI, advertised rates of up to 180 dollars an hour for American cardiologists to write cardiac scenarios and rank the answers of AI models. Comparable work in Tagalog was listed at up to 7.50 dollars an hour, and in Swahili at up to 12.50. Companies that once sought the cheapest labour they could find now court physicians, lawyers and people with doctorates as well.

Posada's argument rests on six years of interviews, most of them in Venezuela, where the economic collapse produced a vast pool of educated people willing to label data for dollars. One former computer science teacher, whom he calls Rogelio, worked alongside his teenage son on platforms such as Hive and Scale's Remotasks; the boy earned 18 cents for a few hours, the father just over two dollars on his first day. A lucrative task briefly lifted the family's takings to 20 dollars in a single day in December 2020, but by early 2021 it had vanished, and their earnings slipped below the five-dollar weekly minimum Hive required before paying out.

What follows, in Posada's telling, is a recognisable cycle: pay generously to assemble a workforce, then trim rates and move elsewhere. Remotasks ended its hourly programme in Venezuela in 2021, and in March 2024 it shut down in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan, citing security protocols; Scale later conceded that Kenyan workers never received the advance notice it said had been sent. The platforms' terms of service, he notes, let the company withhold or delay payment at its own determination and deactivate accounts without warning.

The newer, credentialed recruits appear to be meeting the same logic. Posada draws on reporting by Josh Dzieza, who spoke with more than thirty laid-off lawyers, scientists and screenwriters and heard of mounting demands, shrinking time allowances and falling pay over the life of a project. In one case a designer tagging videos for Meta at 21 dollars an hour lost the work over scope changes, only for the same job to reappear under another name at 16 dollars.

Accountability, meanwhile, dissolves along the supply chain. At a 2024 meeting convened by Partnership on AI and the Fairwork project, the AI firms said they employed no data workers, the outsourcers said their prices were dictated by the AI firms, and no workers were in the room. Courts have begun to intervene, from a Kenyan ruling in 2023 that briefly halted the dismissal of 260 Facebook moderators to a proposed settlement over Scale's platforms and a pending class action alleging that the platform Mercor misclassified more than 30,000 professionals; Scale denies wrongdoing, and the Mercor case is unresolved.

Posada's sharpest point is that the cardiologist and the Venezuelan teacher now share a condition, however far apart their pay. Neither controls the rate, and either can watch a task evaporate overnight. Read from the left, the essay recasts the AI debate as an old question of labour power rather than a new one about machines: the issue is not whether skill survives, but who gets to set its price.

glossary.en: work paid by the unit or task completed rather than by time
able to be ended instantly and without formality
to try to attract or win over
the money earned from work or sales over a period
to admit, often reluctantly, that something is true
according to its own judgement, without external check
holding formal qualifications such as degrees or licences
glossary.zh: 有资质的；有学历证书的

glossary.w: to dissolve along the supply chain
glossary.en: to disappear as responsibility is passed between linked firms
to label workers wrongly, especially as contractors instead of employees
workers' collective capacity to shape pay and conditions
glossary.zh: 劳工力量；劳动者议价能力

items.grammar: The final paragraph uses 'however' as a concessive adverb before an adjective or adverb: 'however far apart their pay'. It means 'no matter how far apart their pay is', and the verb 'to be' is often dropped in formal writing. The structure is 'however + adjective/adverb (+ subject + verb)', as in 'however skilled they are' or 'however hard she tried'.
items.grammar_zh: 最后一段的 'however far apart their pay' 中，however 是让步副词，后接形容词或副词，意思是「无论……多么……」。正式文体中常省略 be 动词，完整形式是 'however far apart their pay is'。结构为「however + 形容词/副词（+ 主语 + 谓语）」，例如 'however skilled they are'（无论他们多有技能）。
questions: Why does Posada locate the origins of the pattern in Venezuela rather than in Silicon Valley?
What does the 2024 meeting reveal about how responsibility is distributed between AI firms and outsourcers?
Is 'extractivism' a convincing metaphor for data work, given that a platform can move tasks in a way an oil field cannot?

sources.title: Julián Posada, 'AI isn't replacing your job. It's turning it into low-paid gig work.' Rest of World, 19 November 2026

items.title: En Antigua Guatemala: ¿dónde está el banco?
items.dek: Una turista le pregunta a un joven cómo llegar al banco en una calle de Antigua Guatemala.
paragraphs: Sofía: Perdón, ¿dónde está el banco?
Tomás: Hola. El banco está en la calle Cuarta, cerca del parque.
Sofía: ¿Está lejos de aquí?
Tomás: No, está a cinco minutos a pie.
Sofía: ¿Y cómo llego?
Tomás: Siga derecho dos cuadras y después doble a la izquierda.
Sofía: Derecho dos cuadras y a la izquierda. ¿Y después?
Tomás: Después ve una iglesia amarilla. El banco está enfrente de la iglesia.
Sofía: ¿Enfrente de la iglesia? Perfecto. ¿Hay un cajero automático también?
Tomás: Sí, hay uno al lado de la puerta.
Sofía: Muchas gracias por su ayuda.
Tomás: De nada. ¡Que le vaya bien!
paragraphs_en: Sorry, where is the bank?
Hi. The bank is on Fourth Street, near the park.
Is it far from here?
No, it's five minutes on foot.
And how do I get there?
Go straight two blocks and then turn left.
Straight two blocks and left. And then?
Then you'll see a yellow church. The bank is in front of the church.
In front of the church? Perfect. Is there an ATM too?
Yes, there is one next to the door.
Thank you very much for your help.
You're welcome. Have a good day!
paragraphs_de: Entschuldigung, wo ist die Bank?
Hallo. Die Bank ist in der Calle Cuarta, in der Nähe des Parks.
Ist es weit von hier?
Nein, es ist fünf Minuten zu Fuß entfernt.
Und wie komme ich hin?
Gehen Sie zwei Blocks geradeaus und biegen Sie dann links ab.
Zwei Blocks geradeaus und links. Und dann?
Dann sehen Sie eine gelbe Kirche. Die Bank liegt gegenüber der Kirche.
Gegenüber der Kirche? Perfekt. Gibt es auch einen Geldautomaten?
Ja, es gibt einen neben der Tür.
Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe.
Gern geschehen. Alles Gute!
items.grammar: To say where something is, use estar: “El banco está en la calle Cuarta.” Add small place words to be exact: cerca de (near), lejos de (far from), enfrente de (in front of), al lado de (next to). Note: de + el becomes del (“al lado del parque”). For “there is/are”, use hay: “Hay un cajero.”
items.grammar_de: Um zu sagen, wo etwas ist, benutzt man estar: „El banco está en la calle Cuarta.“ Kleine Ortswörter machen es genauer: cerca de (nahe bei), lejos de (weit von), enfrente de (gegenüber von), al lado de (neben). Achtung: de + el wird zu del („al lado del parque“). Für „es gibt“ nimmt man hay: „Hay un cajero.“
questions: ¿Y tú? ¿Qué hay cerca de tu casa?

items.title: Galápagos: islas donde los animales no tienen miedo
items.dek: Tortugas gigantes, iguanas que nadan y unas reglas muy claras para los visitantes de Ecuador.
paragraphs: Las islas Galápagos son un grupo de islas del océano Pacífico. Pertenecen a Ecuador, pero están muy lejos del continente. Son islas volcánicas y algunas todavía tienen volcanes activos.

Lo más famoso de las Galápagos son los animales. Allí viven tortugas gigantes, iguanas marinas y pájaros con las patas azules. Muchos de estos animales no viven en ningún otro lugar del mundo. Por eso los científicos las estudian desde hace mucho tiempo.

En 1835, el naturalista inglés Charles Darwin visitó las islas. Observó que los animales de cada isla eran un poco diferentes. Esas ideas lo ayudaron después a escribir sobre la evolución. Hoy mucha gente viaja a las Galápagos para ver ese lugar especial.

Las islas son un parque nacional y un sitio del Patrimonio Mundial de la UNESCO desde 1978. Por eso hay reglas claras para los visitantes. No se puede tocar a los animales ni darles comida. Hay que caminar por los senderos y mantener la distancia. Además, es mejor no llevar plástico y no dejar basura.

Muchos turistas piensan que estas reglas son un poco estrictas, pero tienen una razón simple. Los animales casi no tienen miedo de las personas, y es fácil molestarlos sin querer. Si cuidamos las islas, mañana otras personas también pueden verlas.
Dato curioso: la palabra «galápago» es una palabra antigua del español para una tortuga. De ahí viene el nombre de las islas.
paragraphs_en: The Galápagos Islands are a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean. They belong to Ecuador, but they are very far from the mainland. They are volcanic islands, and some still have active volcanoes.

The most famous thing about the Galápagos is the animals. Giant tortoises, marine iguanas and birds with blue feet live there. Many of these animals live nowhere else in the world. That is why scientists have studied them for a long time.

In 1835, the English naturalist Charles Darwin visited the islands. He noticed that the animals on each island were a little different. Those ideas later helped him write about evolution. Today many people travel to the Galápagos to see this special place.

The islands are a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1978. That is why there are clear rules for visitors. You may not touch the animals or feed them. You have to walk on the paths and keep your distance. It is also better not to bring plastic and not to leave trash.

Many tourists think these rules are a bit strict, but there is a simple reason. The animals are hardly afraid of people, and it is easy to disturb them by accident. If we take care of the islands, other people can see them tomorrow too.
Fun fact: the word “galápago” is an old Spanish word for a tortoise. The islands get their name from it.
paragraphs_de: Die Galápagos-Inseln sind eine Inselgruppe im Pazifik. Sie gehören zu Ecuador, liegen aber sehr weit vom Festland entfernt. Es sind Vulkaninseln, und einige haben noch aktive Vulkane.

Das Berühmteste an den Galápagos sind die Tiere. Dort leben Riesenschildkröten, Meerechsen und Vögel mit blauen Füßen. Viele dieser Tiere leben nirgendwo sonst auf der Welt. Deshalb erforschen Wissenschaftler sie schon lange.

1835 besuchte der englische Naturforscher Charles Darwin die Inseln. Er bemerkte, dass die Tiere auf jeder Insel ein bisschen anders waren. Diese Ideen halfen ihm später, über die Evolution zu schreiben. Heute reisen viele Menschen auf die Galápagos, um diesen besonderen Ort zu sehen.

Die Inseln sind ein Nationalpark und seit 1978 ein UNESCO-Welterbe. Deshalb gibt es klare Regeln für Besucher. Man darf die Tiere nicht berühren und nicht füttern. Man muss auf den Wegen bleiben und Abstand halten. Außerdem ist es besser, kein Plastik mitzunehmen und keinen Müll zu hinterlassen.

Viele Touristen finden diese Regeln ein bisschen streng, aber es gibt einen einfachen Grund. Die Tiere haben kaum Angst vor Menschen, und man stört sie leicht aus Versehen. Wenn wir die Inseln schützen, können sie morgen auch andere Menschen sehen.
Kleine Kuriosität: Das Wort „galápago“ ist ein altes spanisches Wort für eine Schildkröte. Daher kommt der Name der Inseln.
items.grammar: Hay que + infinitive says what is necessary in general, for everyone: “Hay que caminar por los senderos.” For rules and permission, use se puede / no se puede + infinitive: “No se puede tocar a los animales.” Both forms do not need a subject, so they are perfect for signs and instructions.
items.grammar_de: Hay que + Infinitiv sagt, was allgemein für alle nötig ist: „Hay que caminar por los senderos.“ Für Regeln und Erlaubnis benutzt man se puede / no se puede + Infinitiv: „No se puede tocar a los animales.“ Beide Formen brauchen kein Subjekt, deshalb passen sie gut zu Schildern und Anweisungen.
questions: ¿A qué país pertenecen las islas Galápagos?
¿Qué no se puede hacer en las islas?
¿Y tú? ¿Qué animal quieres ver en un viaje?

items.title: A aluna nova
items.dek: Segunda-feira: uma aluna nova na aula de Letras — e ela conhece muito bem um gato laranja.
paragraphs: Segunda-feira, 23 de novembro de 2026. Querido diário, hoje é segunda-feira. De manhã, o Tito come a ração dele e dorme no sofá. Que vida boa!
Às sete da noite, eu chego na aula. Tem uma aluna nova. Ela é alta e simpática. A professora pergunta: — Como você se chama? — Clara. — De onde você é? — De Curitiba.
— O que você faz, Clara? — Sou veterinária. — Onde você trabalha? — Na Clínica Bicho Bom. — Há quanto tempo? — Há dois anos.
Depois da aula, eu pergunto: — Por que você faz Letras, Clara? Ela ri: — Porque os meus pacientes não falam!
Então ela pergunta: — Ana, o seu gato é pequeno e laranja? O nome dele é Tito? — Sim! Como você sabe? — Ele é meu paciente. É pequeno, mas muito bravo!

Às dez e meia da noite, eu volto para casa. Eu falo: — Tito, a sua veterinária é minha colega! O Tito corre para debaixo da cama. Amanhã é terça-feira, dia 24. Boa noite, diário. Boa noite, Tito, meu paciente bravo.
paragraphs_en: Monday, 23 November 2026. Dear diary, today is Monday. In the morning, Tito eats his food and sleeps on the sofa. What a good life!
At seven in the evening, I arrive at class. There is a new student. She is tall and friendly. The teacher asks: "What's your name?" "Clara." "Where are you from?" "From Curitiba."
"What do you do, Clara?" "I'm a vet." "Where do you work?" "At the Bicho Bom clinic." "For how long?" "For two years."
After class, I ask: "Why are you studying Letters, Clara?" She laughs: "Because my patients don't talk!"
Then she asks: "Ana, is your cat small and orange? Is his name Tito?" "Yes! How do you know?" "He's my patient. He's small, but very grumpy!"
At half past ten at night, I go back home. I say: "Tito, your vet is my classmate!" Tito runs under the bed. Tomorrow is Tuesday, the 24th. Good night, diary. Good night, Tito, my grumpy patient.
paragraphs_zh: 2026年11月23日，星期一。亲爱的日记，今天是星期一。早上，蒂托吃完它的饲料，在沙发上睡觉。日子真好！
晚上七点，我到了课上。有一个新同学。她个子高，人很友善。老师问：“你叫什么名字？”“克拉拉。”“你是哪里人？”“库里蒂巴人。”
“克拉拉，你是做什么的？”“我是兽医。”“你在哪里工作？”“在‘好动物’诊所。”“多久了？”“两年了。”
下课后，我问：“克拉拉，你为什么学文学？”她笑着说：“因为我的病人不会说话！”
然后她问：“安娜，你的猫是不是又小又橙？它叫蒂托吗？”“是的！你怎么知道？”“它是我的病人。它个子小，可是脾气很凶！”
晚上十点半，我回家。我说：“蒂托，你的兽医是我的同学！”蒂托跑到床底下去了。明天是星期二，24号。晚安，日记。晚安，蒂托，我的凶巴巴的小病人。
paragraphs_de: Montag, 23. November 2026. Liebes Tagebuch, heute ist Montag. Morgens frisst Tito sein Futter und schläft auf dem Sofa. Was für ein schönes Leben!
Um sieben Uhr abends komme ich zum Unterricht. Es gibt eine neue Studentin. Sie ist groß und sympathisch. Die Lehrerin fragt: „Wie heißt du?“ „Clara.“ „Woher kommst du?“ „Aus Curitiba.“
„Was machst du beruflich, Clara?“ „Ich bin Tierärztin.“ „Wo arbeitest du?“ „In der Klinik Bicho Bom.“ „Seit wann?“ „Seit zwei Jahren.“
Nach dem Unterricht frage ich: „Warum studierst du Literatur, Clara?“ Sie lacht: „Weil meine Patienten nicht sprechen!“
Dann fragt sie: „Ana, ist deine Katze klein und orange? Heißt er Tito?“ „Ja! Woher weißt du das?“ „Er ist mein Patient. Er ist klein, aber sehr grimmig!“

Um halb elf abends gehe ich nach Hause. Ich sage: „Tito, deine Tierärztin ist meine Kommilitonin!“ Tito rennt unter das Bett. Morgen ist Dienstag, der 24. Gute Nacht, Tagebuch. Gute Nacht, Tito, mein grimmiger Patient.

glossary.pt: Pessoa que estuda numa aula: a Clara é uma aluna nova.
Uma pessoa simpática é boa e alegre com os outros.
Quem vai ao médico ou à veterinária: o Tito é paciente da Clara.
Fazer "ha ha ha" quando uma coisa é engraçada.
Pessoa da mesma aula ou do mesmo trabalho.
Ir muito rápido com os pés (ou com as patas!).

items.grammar: Questions about work and study come in a chain: O que você faz? (what do you do?) — Sou veterinária (no article before the job!). To ask "for how long?" say Há quanto tempo? and answer with há + time: Há dois anos (for two years).
items.grammar_zh: 问工作和学习的问题常常一个接一个：O que você faz?（你是做什么的？）—— Sou veterinária（我是兽医；职业前不加冠词！）。问“多久了？”说 Há quanto tempo?，回答用 há + 时间：Há dois anos（两年了）。
items.grammar_de: Fragen zu Beruf und Studium kommen oft hintereinander: O que você faz? (Was machst du beruflich?) — Sou veterinária (ohne Artikel vor dem Beruf!). „Seit wann?“ heißt Há quanto tempo?, die Antwort ist há + Zeit: Há dois anos (seit zwei Jahren).
items.grammar_pt: Perguntas sobre trabalho e estudo vêm uma depois da outra: O que você faz? — Sou veterinária (sem artigo antes da profissão!). Para perguntar o tempo, use Há quanto tempo? e responda com há + tempo: Há dois anos.
questions: Qual é a profissão da Clara? Onde ela trabalha?
Por que a Clara faz Letras?
E você? O que você faz? Há quanto tempo?
